title: Wait for the Whole Story Before You Call It
summary: The first version of what went wrong is usually too clean. Why hindsight fools us, how blameless postmortems handle it, and how to put a clock on waiting for context.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Friday afternoon, a status update lands: the payments migration has slipped two weeks. From where you sit, the story writes itself. The team was slow, someone underestimated, maybe the lead isn't on top of it. You start drafting a message with the word "accountability" in it.

By Monday the story looks different. The vendor's sandbox was down for four days. Ownership of the webhook service changed hands mid-sprint and nobody updated the tracker. An API the team depended on changed twice. And sales had promised one customer a feature that never made it into a ticket, so the team squeezed it in. The Friday version wasn't exactly wrong. It was thin.

This post is about the gap between the first story and the real one: why it's so tempting to close that gap early, and how to give the missing pieces time to show up without waiting forever.

Why the first story is always too clean

Some impatience feels like decisiveness. It wants a label fast: process problem, people problem, bad design, cut the feature. Sometimes that instinct is right. Often it's just early.

Part of the reason is that context arrives unevenly. One person has the customer history. Another knows the deploy constraint. Someone remembers the option the team dropped last quarter, and someone else has the metric that changes the whole debate. If the first loud interpretation wins, the team never gets to put those pieces together.

Hindsight makes it worse. In How Complex Systems Fail, Richard Cook calls hindsight bias "the primary obstacle to accident investigation." Once you know how things turned out, the warning signs look obvious, far more obvious than they were to the people in the middle of it. Cook also argues that failures have several contributors, none of them enough on its own, and that pinning everything on one "root cause" says more about our need to blame something than about how the failure happened.

Frustration narrows the story

Patience matters most when emotions run high. Frustration turns ambiguity into motive. Why did they do this? Why did nobody think? Why is this always broken? Those questions often carry real pain, and they're worth hearing. They just rarely draw an accurate map on the first try.

Google's SRE teams build their postmortems around this problem. The postmortem culture chapter of their book says a blameless postmortem focuses on the contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team," and assumes everyone involved "had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had." The last part is the one to remember: the information they had at the time, which is usually less than you have now.

Pauses that fit in one sentence

A good pause can be tiny:

  • "Let me check the timeline before I reply."
  • "What do we actually know, and what are we filling in?"
  • "Who was closest to this decision? Let's ask them first."
  • "Is there an older constraint we're forgetting?"

None of these lets anyone off the hook. Accountability gets fairer when it's attached to what happened instead of to the first guess. It also gets more useful, because a fix aimed at the real cause has a chance of working. A fix aimed at the visible symptom can leave the hidden cause right where it was.

Put a clock on the wait

Waiting can also become a way to dodge a hard conversation, so give it edges. Something like: "We'll gather context until 3 p.m. We need three facts: when the vendor outage started, who owned the webhook service and what was promised to the customer. If we still don't know by then, we'll pick the safest option we can reverse." With a clock and a question, patience turns into a plan.

That last clause matters. If the context doesn't arrive in time, a choice you can undo keeps the cost of being wrong low (more on that in Find the Way Back Before You Decide). And if the uncertainty sticks around for weeks, it helps to carry it openly and keep working.

When the context does arrive, the answer may still be hard. Someone may really have dropped the ball. But the conversation is usually less dramatic, and the decision becomes about the next honest step instead of defending a first impression.

Try this week

  • Next time something goes wrong, write the timeline before you write the message.
  • Split your notes into two columns: what we know and what we're assuming.
  • Ask the person closest to the decision before you ask their manager.
  • When you decide to wait, say out loud until when, and which facts you're waiting for.

faqs.q: What is hindsight bias at work?
faqs.a: Once you know how something turned out, the warning signs look obvious, much more than they were to the people involved at the time. Richard Cook calls it the primary obstacle to accident investigation, and it pushes teams toward blaming individuals.

faqs.q: How long should you wait for context before deciding?
faqs.a: Set a deadline and a short list of facts you need. If those facts are still missing at the deadline, choose the safest option you can reverse and keep watching for new information.

faqs.q: What does a blameless postmortem assume?
faqs.a: In Google's SRE practice, a blameless postmortem focuses on contributing causes without indicting any individual or team. It assumes everyone had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had.

faqs.q: Does waiting for context weaken accountability?
faqs.a: No. It makes accountability fairer, because it attaches to what actually happened instead of the first guess, and the fix is more likely to address the real cause instead of only the visible symptom.
